metadata.title: A versatile genetic engineering toolkit for E. coli based on CRISPR-prime editing

reference.title: A versatile genetic engineering toolkit for E. coli based on CRISPR-prime editing

target.condition: LB agar plates with antibiotics (spectinomycin 50 µg/mL, ampicillin 100 µg/mL, chloramphenicol 25 µg/mL), 37 °C, 24 h incubation with 200 ng/mL ATc

trigger.observation: CRISPR base editors are restricted to single-nucleotide substitutions and narrow editing windows; DSB-based CRISPR-Cas9 causes cell death in bacteria lacking NHEJ; prime editing demonstrated in eukaryotes offers potential solution
trigger.reasoning: Validate that CRISPR-Prime Editing system can perform diverse DNA engineering events (insertion, deletion, substitution, combinatorial) on plasmid DNA in E. coli

evidence.source_location: No PEgRNA control; non-induced (no ATc) control

decision_chain.evidence_grading_rationale: 模型自评(软): 见 ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale——需人工确认 | 软 (soft) = predictive. The initial design was based on analogy to eukaryotic PE systems (Anzalone et al. 2019, Lin et al. 2020) and the hypothesis that single-strand nicking would not be lethal in bacteria. This was a prediction requiring experimental validation in the bacterial context.

alternatives.approach: CRISPR base editors (restricted to substitutions, narrow window)
CRISPR-Cas9 with DSB (lethal in bacteria lacking NHEJ)
Recombineering/MAGE (requires specific genetic backgrounds, lower efficiency or fidelity)

decision_chain.implementation_detail: Transformation with three-plasmid system (pCDF-GFPplus reporter, pPEgRNA expressing guide targeting GFP, pCRISPR-PE expressing Cas9n-M-MLV2 fusion) programmed for four editing types: (1) TAA 3-bp insertion, (2) T to A 1-bp substitution, (3) T 1-bp deletion, (4) combinatorial edit; induction with 200 ng/mL ATc for 24 h

result.metric: GFP fluorescence loss (non-green colonies) as proxy for editing; Sanger sequencing to confirm designed edits
result.after: Non-green colonies observed for all four editing types after 24 h induction; almost all Sanger-sequenced clones carried designed stop codon edits (Fig. 2a); target-adjacent unintended indels (indels near target nucleotide) observed in 8/24 clones of 1 bp substitution event, but not in other editing types (Fig. 2b)

decision_chain.rule: When adapting eukaryotic genome editing tools for bacteria, single-strand nicking systems (e.g., prime editing) are likely to be less toxic and more applicable than double-strand break systems (e.g., CRISPR-Cas9), because most bacteria lack NHEJ and DSBs are lethal.

target.condition: LB agar plates with antibiotics and varying ATc concentrations, 37 °C, 24 h

trigger.observation: Cas9n-M-MLV2 fusion is under tetracycline-inducible promoter; need to determine optimal induction level
trigger.reasoning: Determine optimal inducer (ATc) concentration for CRISPR-PE system activation
trigger.source_location: E. coli DH10B harboring three-plasmid system

decision_chain.evidence_grading_rationale: 模型自评(硬): 见 ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale——需人工确认 | 硬 (hard) = empirical measurement. Dose-response was directly measured experimentally.
decision_chain.implementation_detail: Induction with eight different ATc concentrations: 0, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000 ng/mL for four editing events (3 bp insertion, 1 bp deletion, 1 bp substitution, combinatorial)

result.after: Dose-dependent induction observed for all editing types; at 1000 ng/mL: 1 bp deletion 43.7%, 3 bp insertion 13.8%, 1 bp substitution 19.9%, combinatorial 2.1%; efficiency did not change significantly between 100-500 ng/mL, so 200 ng/mL chosen as standard

decision_chain.rule: When optimizing inducible CRISPR systems, identify the dose-response plateau region and select a concentration within this range to balance efficiency and potential toxicity.

target.condition: LB agar plates with antibiotics, 200 ng/mL ATc, 37 °C, 24 h

trigger.observation: Initial PEgRNA design (13 nt PBS, 13 nt RTT) based on eukaryotic studies; need to determine if optimal in bacterial context
trigger.reasoning: Optimize primer binding site (PBS) and reverse transcription template (RTT) lengths for maximum editing efficiency
trigger.source_location: E. coli DH10B harboring three-plasmid system

evidence.source_location: Baseline with initial 13 nt PBS and 13 nt RTT

decision_chain.evidence_grading_rationale: 模型自评(硬): 见 ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale——需人工确认 | 硬 (hard) = empirical measurement. Length optimization was directly tested experimentally.
decision_chain.implementation_detail: PBS length variants: 5, 8, 13, 17 nt; RTT scaffold length variants: 4, 5, 8, 13, 20 nt; tested for TAA-STOP codon insertion editing; induction with 200 ng/mL ATc

result.after: PBS: nearly no edits with 5 or 8 nt; 17 nt equivalent to 13 nt; functional window 13-17 nt. RTT: too short (<10 nt) or too long (>20 nt) reduced efficiency; optimal ~13 nt.

decision_chain.rule: When designing PEgRNAs for prime editing in bacteria, use a PBS of 13-17 nt and an RTT scaffold of approximately 13 nt, as these lengths balance binding stability, editing window accessibility, and reverse transcription efficiency.

target.condition: LB agar plates with antibiotics, 200 ng/mL ATc, 37 °C, 24 h

trigger.observation: Need to define the practical range of edit sizes achievable with the toolkit
trigger.reasoning: Determine size limits for DNA fragment insertion and deletion using CRISPR-PE system
trigger.source_location: E. coli DH10B harboring three-plasmid system

evidence.source_location: Baseline 3 bp insertion and 1 bp deletion

decision_chain.evidence_grading_rationale: 模型自评(硬): 见 ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale——需人工确认 | 硬 (hard) = empirical measurement. Size capacity was directly tested experimentally.
decision_chain.implementation_detail: Designed insertions: 3, 12, 18, 33 bp; designed deletions: 1, 10, 23, 36, 49, 97 bp; induction with 200 ng/mL ATc

result.after: All designed insertions and deletions (up to 33 bp and 97 bp, respectively) could be obtained, but efficiency dropped sharply with size. At 200 ng/mL ATc: 1 bp deletion 29.5%, 10 bp deletion 17.8%, 23-97 bp deletions <2%; 3 bp insertion ~10%, 18-33 bp insertions <1%. Insertion generally less efficient than deletion.

decision_chain.rule: When using prime editing for bacterial genome engineering, expect high efficiency for small edits (1-10 bp) and sharp efficiency decline for larger edits (>20 bp); plan for lower success rates or increased screening effort when designing edits >20 bp.

target.condition: For lacZ: LB plates with X-gal (40 µL of 20 mg/mL per plate) and antibiotics, 200 ng/mL ATc, 37 °C; for galK: M63 minimal medium plates with 0.1% 2-DOG for positive selection

trigger.observation: Successful plasmid editing demonstrated; need to test if system works on chromosomal DNA
trigger.reasoning: Assess ability of CRISPR-PE system to edit chromosomal DNA in E. coli

evidence.source_location: WT E. coli MG1655 (for lacZ phenotype comparison); non-induced controls

decision_chain.evidence_grading_rationale: 模型自评(硬): 见 ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale——需人工确认 | 硬 (hard) = empirical measurement. Chromosomal editing was directly tested and validated.
decision_chain.implementation_detail: For lacZ: designed early stop codon introduction via TAG insertion, GC deletion, or GT to TA substitution (three separate experiments); for galK: designed TAA stop codon insertion; induction with 200 ng/mL ATc

result.metric: For lacZ: white vs. blue colonies on X-gal plates (editing efficiency = white/total); for galK: colony formation on 2-DOG plates; Sanger sequencing confirmation
result.after: lacZ editing efficiencies: substitution 6.8%, insertion 12.2%, deletion 26%; all Sanger-sequenced non-blue colonies (8 per type) bore expected edits. galK: all 4 colonies from 2-DOG plate showed expected TAA insertion.

target.condition: LB agar plates with antibiotics, 200 ng/mL ATc, 37 °C, 24 h

trigger.reasoning: Assess capability for multiplexed editing using two PEgRNAs

decision_chain.evidence_grading_rationale: 模型自评(硬): 见 ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale——需人工确认 | 硬 (hard) = empirical measurement. Multiplexing was directly tested.

alternatives.approach: PEgRNA self-processing machinery like Csy4 (mentioned in Discussion as future direction)

decision_chain.implementation_detail: Introduction of fourth plasmid pVRb_PEgRNA (pSC101 ori, KanR) carrying second PEgRNA for G deletion, into cells already harboring three-plasmid system programmed for TAA insertion, T deletion, T to A substitution, two Ts to two Cs substitution, or combinatory editing; induction with 200 ng/mL ATc

result.metric: Sanger sequencing to identify clones with both designed edits (two nicks 111 bp apart)
result.after: All expected dual-editing events successfully identified (Fig. 2c), but editing efficiency was relatively low (<1%)

decision_chain.rule: When multiplexing prime editing in bacteria, delivering multiple PEgRNAs from separate compatible plasmids can achieve simultaneous editing, but expect low efficiency (<1%); further optimization of PEgRNA processing or delivery is needed for practical multiplexing.

target.condition: LB agar plates with antibiotics, 200 ng/mL ATc, 37 °C

trigger.observation: Second nick in non-edited strand increases PE efficiency in some mammalian and plant cells (refs 19, 20)
trigger.reasoning: Test whether introducing a second nick in the non-edited strand increases editing efficiency (as observed in some mammalian and plant cells)

decision_chain.evidence_grading_rationale: 模型自评(硬): 见 ddr_annotation.evidence_grading_rationale——需人工确认 | 硬 (hard) = empirical measurement. Second nick strategies were directly tested.
decision_chain.implementation_detail: Designed and validated two strategies for second nick introduction (details in Supplementary Note 1); co-transformation with plasmid expressing second nicking sgRNA (pnsgRNA) alongside PE system

result.after: Almost no visible colonies after second nick introduction; second nick does not increase efficiency in E. coli and instead compromises the system, likely due to absence of NHEJ leading to DSB-like lethality

decision_chain.rule: When adapting prime editing enhancements from eukaryotes to bacteria, be cautious with strategies that introduce additional nicks or breaks, as bacteria lacking NHEJ may not tolerate them; test viability first before assessing efficiency gains.

evidence.quote: CAC codon. We obtained eight non-fluorescent clones out of which six clones were correctly edited (Supplementary Fig. 2). To further assess whether CRISPR-Prime Editing system for E. coli is capable of multiplexed editing, we introduced another compatible plasmid pVRb carrying a second PEgRNA for a G deletion (pVRb\_PEgRNA\_312Gdel) into E. coli DH10B harboring the 3-plasmid system for TAA insertion, T deletion, T to an A substitution, two Ts to two Cs substitution, and combinatory editing. We successfully identified all expected dual-editing events (Fig. 2c), however the editing efficiency was relatively low (<1%).

Assessing the ability of chromosomal DNA editing with CRISPR-Prime Editing system in E. coli. Beyond editing plasmid DNA, we also assessed if CRISPR-Prime Editing system is capable of engineering chromosomal DNA in E. coli. To this end, two metabolic pathways for lactose and D-galactose degradation in E. coli MG1655 were selected. β-galactosidase, encoded by the lacZ gene within the lactose metabolic pathway, metabolizes X-gal (5-bromo-4-chloro-3-indolyl-β-D-galactoside, an analog of lactose) into 5-bromo-4-chloro-indoxyl, which will form dark blue 5,5<sup>′</sup>-dibromo-4,4<sup>′</sup>-dichloro-indigo by oxidation. On the contrary, X-gal remains colorless if the lacZ gene is inactivated (Fig. 4a, b). An early stop codon was designed to be introduced into the lacZ gene of E. coli MG1655 by insertion of TAG, deletion of GC, and substitution of GT to TA. In general, the editing efficiencies similar to those for plasmid DNA engineering were observed by counting the white colonies out of the total formed colonies on X-gal supplemented LB plates (Fig. 4c). Editing efficiencies of substitution, insertion, and deletion were 6.8%, 12.2%, and 26%, respectively. To validate the editing events, the targeted region of eight randomly picked non-blue colonies from each designed DNA engineering event were PCR amplified and further subjected to Sanger sequencing. All sequenced clones bore the expected edits (Fig. 4d–f). Moreover, another gene, the galK gene from the Leloir pathway of D-galactose metabolism in E. coli MG1655 was tested. The loss of function of the galK gene can be positively selected by supplementing a galactose analog 2-deoxy-D-galactose (2-DOG), as 2-DOG will be metabolized by galactokinase (encoded by the galK gene) to form a toxic compound 2- deoxy-galactose-1-phosphate, which cannot be further metabolized<sup>22</sup> (Fig. 4g, h). A TAA stop codon was designed to be inserted into the galK gene in E. coli MG1655 strain. Of the visible colonies on the 2-DOG supplemented M63 agar plate, all four that were randomly picked showed the expected insertion (Fig. 4i).

High throughput electroporation of multiple plasmids. In vivo assay of strains carrying multiple plasmids were performed from freshly transformed E. coli DH10β strains. A HT Nucleofector™ System (Lonza, Switzerland) together with 96- well Nucleocuvette plates (Lonza, Switzerland) were used for high throughput electroporation. Before electroporation, the 96-well Nucleocuvette plate was transferred from −20 °C to ice for 10 min. Twenty microliter of electrocompetent DH10β or MG1655 E. coli cells with 10% glycerol were added into each desired well, 0.5 µL of each plasmid (about 30 ng) was subsequently added. A total amount of plasmid DNA of <100 ng per transformation normally performed well. The program used in this study is X\_bacteria\_14, with the code GN-100. After electroporation, 180 µL of fresh LB broth were added into each well. The cultures were then transferred into a 96-deep well plate containing 200 µL of fresh LB broth (making the transformation culture in total 400 µL) for recovery for 1 h at 37 °C and 300 rpm.

The illumina reads obtained from the sequenced samples were trimmed using Trim Galore (v. 0.6.4\_dev, Cutadapt v. 2.10) with the switches --length 100 and --quality 20. All mutation calls were performed using breseq (v. 0.33.2, bowtie2 v. 2.3.4.1)<sup>23,39</sup> with default parameters. For plasmid-based editing, the E. coli DH10B genome sequence NC\_010473 is used as the reference, while for chromosomebased editing, the E. coli MG1655 genome sequence NC\_ U00096 is used as the reference, both along with the relevant plasmids. Mutation calls that existed in all samples as well as the parental strain were not counted as off-target effects.

extraction_meta.engineering_paper_type_rationale: The paper develops a genome engineering toolkit (prime editing) applicable to metabolic engineering and strain development. The GFP-based screening assay functions as a biosensor platform for editing detection. While not a metabolic engineering study per se (no specific metabolite production), the toolkit is explicitly framed as enabling metabolic engineering and DBTL cycles. The biosensor aspect (GFP fluorescence loss as readout) is central to the screening workflow.

rule_provenance.rule: When adapting eukaryotic genome editing tools for bacteria, single-strand nicking systems (e.g., prime editing) are likely to be less toxic and more applicable than double-strand break systems (e.g., CRISPR-Cas9), because most bacteria lack NHEJ and DSBs are lethal.
When optimizing inducible CRISPR systems, identify the dose-response plateau region and select a concentration within this range to balance efficiency and potential toxicity.

When designing PEgRNAs for prime editing in bacteria, use a PBS of 13-17 nt and an RTT scaffold of approximately 13 nt, as these lengths balance binding stability, editing window accessibility, and reverse transcription efficiency.

When using prime editing for bacterial genome engineering, expect high efficiency for small edits (1-10 bp) and sharp efficiency decline for larger edits (>20 bp); plan for lower success rates or increased screening effort when designing edits >20 bp.

When multiplexing prime editing in bacteria, delivering multiple PEgRNAs from separate compatible plasmids can achieve simultaneous editing, but expect low efficiency (<1%); further optimization of PEgRNA processing or delivery is needed for practical multiplexing.

When adapting prime editing enhancements from eukaryotes to bacteria, be cautious with strategies that introduce additional nicks or breaks, as bacteria lacking NHEJ may not tolerate them; test viability first before assessing efficiency gains.
